title.narrative: Implementation of the La Plata Basin SAP priorities through regional and national actions

description.narrative: Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

Socio-economic BenefitsThe La Plata Basin is one of the largest and most strategic river systems in the world. It provides water for domestic use, agriculture, fisheries, energy, and navigation, supporting the livelihoods of millions of people across five countries. Its role in global water and food security [1]is critical, but it faces increasing pressures from climate change and variability, pollution, ecosystem degradation, and unsustainable land use. Based on the La Plata Basin Strategic Action Program (SAP), the project will strengthen regional cooperation by enhancing the technical capacity of the CIC Plata General Secretariat and the national water-related agencies, improving coordination, technical cooperation, and joint planning. This will positively impact on use agreements, sustainable access to water-related services and the development of joint solutions with shared benefits. A revolving fund will be established to facilitate the preparation and implementation of new projects, ensuring agile and sustained access to international and national financing. This will provide continuity and sustainability to the implementation of the SAP through investments in infrastructure, ecological restoration, monitoring, and climate adaptation, generating employment, promoting local development, and reducing dependence on external funding cycles. At the territorial level, replicable “implementation initiatives” with high social and environmental impact will be executed, generating direct improvements in living conditions and local economies. In the Gran Chaco, access to water for Indigenous communities such as the Wichí, Guaraní, and Qom will be improved by integrating traditional knowledge with systems for water capture, storage, and treatment. These interventions will help reduce exposure to waterborne diseases, strengthen community autonomy, and ensure basic conditions for food production, health, and well-being. In the Ñeembucú–Iberá wetlands, the mitigation of eutrophication through artificial wetlands, water treatment, and sustainable farming practices will support ecological restoration, artisanal fishing, tourism, and ecosystem services[2], generating income, diversifying livelihoods, and boosting local economies through environmentally compatible activities. In the recovering micro-basins of Bolivia and the Brazilian Cerrado, restoration practices, erosion control, and reforestation will increase water infiltration, reduce flood impacts, and strengthen local agroecological systems. These interventions will support the productive recovery of rural areas, create sustainable jobs, improve water availability for agricultural and domestic use, and enhance community climate resilience. In the Uruguay River and the Río de la Plata, monitoring networks, early warning systems, and forecasting tools will be designed and implemented to improve response capacity to extreme events, reduce health risks, and strengthen the safety of key sectors such as fisheries, transportation, and coastal activities. A central focus will be the sustainable management of groundwater. The project will update the diagnosis of national aquifers, design management plans and monitoring networks in priority sites, and promote a systemic approach integrating the relationship between groundwater, surface water, and dependent ecosystems. This integration will improve the protection of water sources, conserve wetlands, strengthen natural recharge, and ensure a more stable supply for human consumption, production, and environmental sustainability. The benefits will particularly reach dispersed rural communities, Indigenous Peoples, and populations in arid zones, improving their water security, reducing climate risk exposure, and strengthening the ecosystem services they depend on for their well-being and livelihoods. Quantitatively, and in direct alignment with GEF Core Indicators 3, 4, and 11, the project is expected to benefit more than 200,000 people directly—at least 50% of whom will be women—through improved water access, job creation in restoration and monitoring, and participation in training and management processes. The initiatives will cover approximately 420,900 hectares of restored land, promote sustainable practices across more than 500,000 hectares, and enhance climate resilience in highly vulnerable rural and Indigenous areas. These impacts will serve as enabling conditions for sustainable water management and for consolidating transboundary cooperation. All benefits will be systematically monitored and reported during project implementation and assessed in the Mid-Term Review (MTR) and Terminal Evaluation Report (TER), in accordance with GEF guidelines. [1] Water Security. Argentina accepts the IHP UNESCO Phase VIII definition: the ability of a given population to safeguard access to adequate quantities of water of acceptable quality to sustain both human and ecosystem health, based on watersheds, as well as to ensure the protection of life and property against water-related hazards - floods, landslides, soil subsidence and drought. [2] Ecosystem services. According to its current regulations, Bolivia does not agree with the commodification of nature, so it does not recognise the term "ecosystem services", nor can it support activities with payment or compensation schemes for environmental functions.

To foster transboundary cooperation and regional integration in the management of freshwater resources in the Plata Basin, aiming to achieve sustainable development in the Basin countries and enhance the welfare of their populations.
